title: Comparing two set-ups across seeds
objectives: Compare two training set-ups across seeds with a paired test and a confidence interval.

screens.title: Ten seeds each
screens.prose: Set-up A is our net with Adam at 0.01; set-up B raises the rate to 0.015. Each ran with seeds 0 to 9, and each seed gave A and B the same starting weights and batches. A averages 0.108 (sd 0.046); B averages 0.088 (sd 0.044).
screens.question: Is B's lower loss real, or seed noise?

options.text: Probably real: B is lower on every seed, and each pair shares its seed
Noise: the means differ by 0.021, less than either sd
options.why: The sds measure how much one run moves with its seed; here both runs of a pair move together, so that noise cancels in the pair.

options.text: Cannot say: ten seeds are too few for any claim
options.why: Ten pairs can be plenty when the pairs agree this well.

hints.text: Look at each seed's two bars side by side.
Within a seed, which bar is lower?
B is lower on 10 of 10 seeds.

feedback.correct: B wins on all 10 seeds: the seed moves both bars, and B sits lower within each pair.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the bars within each seed.

byKey.noise: The seed-to-seed spread is shared by A and B, so it cancels within a pair.
byKey.few: Ten agreeing pairs carry a lot of evidence.

explain.text: Hard seeds are hard for both set-ups: seed 7 gives about 0.20 to each. Within every pair B is lower. Comparing within pairs removes the seed noise that swamps the two means.

screens.title: Pairs against the diagonal
screens.prose: Each point is one seed: A's loss across, B's up. On the dashed line B equals A; below it, B won. The points spread along the line, which is the seed noise, but sit below it.
screens.question: Tap the seed where B gained most over A.

hints.text: The gain is the drop below the line.
Look for the point farthest under the diagonal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Measure the drop below the dashed line, not the height.

byKey.p7: Seed 7 is the hardest seed for both; B gains little there.

explain.text: Along the line the seeds range from about 0.06 to 0.20; below it, the gaps are small but all on one side. The paired test works with those gaps alone.

screens.title: The paired test
screens.prose: Name it: give A and B the same seed each time, so each pair shares its weights and batches, and test the differences $d_i = b_i - a_i$. As in `testing` l8, $$t = \frac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt n},$$ with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.
screens.question: Our ten differences have mean -0.0206 and sd 0.0180. What is $t$? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Then divide the mean difference by that.

feedback.correct: $-0.0206/0.00569 = -3.62$ from the rounded figures and $-3.63$ from the unrounded runs, on 9 degrees of freedom.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide $\bar d$ by $s_d/\sqrt n$.

byKey.sign: B minus A is negative here: keep the sign.
byKey.nosqrt: You divided by $s_d$ alone; the standard error is $s_d/\sqrt n$.

explain.text: The standard error of $\bar d$ is $0.0180/\sqrt{10} = 0.00569$, so $\bar d$ is about 3.6 of them below 0. SciPy's `ttest_rel` on the unrounded runs gives $t = -3.63$ and $p = 0.0055$.

screens.title: By hand, five pairs
screens.prose: Seeds 0 to 4 only. Their differences, B minus A, to 3 places: -0.016, -0.016, -0.011, -0.023, -0.063.
screens.question: Find $\bar d$, $s_d$ and $t$. Give 4 decimal places for the first two and 2 for $t$.

hints.text: Mean of the five, then the sd with $n - 1 = 4$.

feedback.correct: $\bar d = -0.0258$, $s_d = 0.0212$, $t = -2.72$ on 4 degrees of freedom, $p = 0.053$: five pairs fall just short where ten were clear.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Mean, sd over $n - 1$, then $t$.

byKey.dsign: Keep the minus signs: B was lower.
byKey.tsign: The differences are negative, so $t$ is too.

explain.text: Mean -0.0258; seed 4's large gap makes the sd 0.0212. Then $t = -0.0258/(0.0212/\sqrt 5) = -2.72$.

screens.title: The unpaired test
screens.prose: Now ignore the pairing: treat A and B as two independent groups of ten. Run Welch's test of `testing` l8 on the same twenty numbers, with A at 0.1085 (sd 0.0457) and B at 0.0879 (sd 0.0439).
screens.question: What is Welch's $t$? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Divide B's mean minus A's by it.

feedback.correct: $t = -1.03$ and $p = 0.32$: the same runs, with the pairing thrown away, look like nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the gap in means by the combined standard error.

byKey.paired: That is the paired $t$; Welch uses the two groups' own sds.

explain.text: Welch divides the gap by $0.0201$, which is full of seed noise, so $t = -1.03$ and $p = 0.32$. The paired test divides by $0.0057$ and gets $p = 0.0055$. Same numbers; less power.

screens.title: The interval
screens.prose: The 95% confidence interval for the mean difference is $\bar d \pm t_{0.975,\,9}\, s_d/\sqrt n$, with $t_{0.975,\,9} = 2.262$. Here $\bar d = -0.0206$ and $s_d = 0.0180$.
screens.question: What is the upper end of the interval? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: That is 0.0129 from the rounded figures.

feedback.correct: $-0.0206 + 0.0129 = -0.0077$ from the rounded figures, or $-0.0078$ from the unrounded runs: either way the interval, about -0.0334 to -0.0078, stays below 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the half-width to $\bar d$.

byKey.sign: The upper end is still below 0: keep the minus sign.
byKey.z: With 9 degrees of freedom use 2.262, not 1.96.

explain.text: From the unrounded runs the interval runs from -0.0334 to -0.0078, below 0 throughout. So for new seeds on this split, B's rate lowers the mean loss by between 0.008 and 0.033. That is the sentence to write, more than the $p$-value.

screens.title: Twenty set-ups
screens.prose: A team tries 20 learning rates against the baseline, each with its own paired test at 5%. Suppose none truly differs from the baseline and the tests are independent, as in `testing` l9.
screens.question: What is the chance that at least one shows a "significant" win? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Find the chance that none passes first.

feedback.generic: Not quite. One minus the chance that all twenty fail.

byKey.sum: Adding 20 times 5% double counts; take one minus the chance of no pass.

explain.text: All twenty fail with chance $0.95^{20} = 0.358$, so at least one passes with chance 0.642. Tests against one shared baseline are not quite independent, so the true chance is a little lower. A Bonferroni correction (`testing` l10) tests each at $0.05/20 = 0.0025$.

screens.title: The wrong test
screens.prose: A colleague compares A and B with an unpaired test, finds $p = 0.32$, and writes "no difference between the rates". Another colleague ran one seed of each and saw B ahead.
screens.question: What is the right reading?

options.text: The runs share seeds, so test the ten differences: $p = 0.0055$, and across seeds B is better on this split
No difference: an unpaired test of all twenty runs is the most cautious
options.why: Caution is not the issue: the unpaired test ignores the pairing, so it measures the gap against seed noise that cancels in each pair.

options.text: B is better: the one-seed run already showed it
options.why: One pair is one draw of the difference; seed 8's gap was almost 0.

hints.text: Each seed gave A and B the same weights and batches.
Paired runs need the paired test, over several pairs.

feedback.correct: Paired runs, paired test, over all ten pairs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how the runs were made.

byKey.nodiff: An unpaired test on paired runs throws the pairing away.
byKey.one: One pair cannot measure a spread.

explain.text: The unpaired $p = 0.32$ answers a question about independent groups, which these are not. A single pair could have been seed 8, where B led by 0.0004. Test all ten differences.

screens.title: Edge case: batches not fixed
screens.prose: Rerun B with the same starting weights but its batches drawn from another seed, so pairs share only their weights. The correlation between A and B falls from 0.92 to 0.65; the differences now have mean -0.0244 and sd 0.0346.
screens.question: What is the paired $t$ now? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Same formula, new mean and sd.
Divide the new mean by that.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the new mean and sd.

byKey.old: That is the $t$ with shared batches.
byKey.sign: B is still lower on average: $t$ is negative.

explain.text: With different batches the pairs share less noise, so $s_d$ nearly doubles, from 0.0180 to 0.0346. Then $t = -2.22$ and $p = 0.053$, against 0.0055 before. Fix every stream you can.

screens.title: A paired comparison in code
screens.prose: Write `paired_t(a, b)`, returning $\bar d$, $t$ and the 95% interval for $d = b - a$, and `compare_configs(runs, a, b)`, which pairs two set-ups' runs by seed and reports `n`, `mean_diff`, `t`, `ci` and `wins`.
screens.question: Write both functions.

Then A against B and against B with other batches, a file with two of B's seeds missing, and a win count. Values within relative $10^{-9}$.

Uses the unpaired standard error on paired runs.
Uses the normal 1.96 instead of the t quantile.
Pairs by position, so missing seeds shift the pairs.

The interval uses `t_quantile(0.975, n - 1)` times $s_d/\sqrt n$.
Key each set-up's losses by seed and keep the seeds both have.

screens.title: How many seeds
screens.prose: As in `testing` l6, the pairs needed for power $1 - \beta$ at a two-sided level $\alpha$ are about $n = \big((z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})\, s_d/\delta\big)^2$, rounded up. Write `runs_needed(sd_d, delta, alpha, power)`; `NormalDist().inv_cdf` gives $z$.
screens.question: Write `runs_needed`.

screens.title: For the investment committee
screens.prose: Two versions of a signal model were trained on the same 8 seeds. Version 2 minus version 1, in out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, has mean 0.12 and sd 0.10 across the pairs. Take $t_{0.975,\,7} = 2.365$.
screens.question: What is the lower end of the 95% interval for the mean gain? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Mean minus the half-width.

byKey.z: Eight pairs: use the $t$ quantile, not 1.96.

explain.text: The interval is 0.036 to 0.204. The sentence: "on 8 shared seeds and one test period, version 2 raised out-of-sample Sharpe by 0.12, with a 95% interval of 0.04 to 0.20." It covers seed noise only: both versions saw one test period, whose own noise (`testing` l11) it leaves out.

ideas: Give both set-ups the same seed each time, so each pair shares its weights and batches, and test the differences.
Our A and B differ by less than either sd, yet the paired test gives $t = -3.63$ and an interval of -0.0334 to -0.0078; Welch on the same runs gives $p = 0.32$.
Trying many set-ups is multiple testing: twenty independent tests at 5% give about a 64% chance of a false win.

formula.name: Paired test across seeds
formula.tex: t = \dfrac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt n}, \qquad \bar d \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\,\dfrac{s_d}{\sqrt n}
formula.note: $d_i = b_i - a_i$ on seed $i$; $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.

summary.trap: An unpaired test on paired runs, or a win declared from one seed pair.

Welch's test on the two groups of ten
